title: AI-MBE Benchmark: A study to determine which generative A.I. model is best at answering multiple choice MBE questions
author: University of Hawaiʻi William S. Richardson School of Law Tech Incubator

dom.t: Benchmark interpretation: Partial success can hide task failure

st.t: Benchmark interpretation: Partial success can hide task failure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s bounded-comparison proposition by reporting a leading score on a specific multiple-choice MBE benchmark, without treating that result as complete legal-task success or readiness for legal practice. Its listing of two Claude 3.5 Sonnet versions without identifying which achieved the winning score also reinforces the need to distinguish model versions when interpreting results.
qs: The best performer was Antropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet which answered 181 questions correctly out of 210 possible questions.

mo.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success

kp.k: Benchmark tests models on 210 sample MBE questions
kp.d: The William S. Richardson School of Law study benchmarks AI performance on the multiple-choice Multistate Bar Exam (MBE). Its methodology describes 16 models from Open AI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic answering 210 sample questions obtained from the National Conference of Bar Examiners (NCBE). The stated task is answering examination questions, rather than delivering legal services.
qs: This project is a benchmarking of different AI models to see which one is the best at solving the multiple choice section of the bar exam known as the Multistate Bar Exam (MBE).
The study was conducted on 16 models from Open AI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic.
The models were asked to solve 210 sample MBE questions obtained from the National Conference of Bar Examiners

kp.k: Claude 3.5 Sonnet led the reported results
kp.d: The repository reports Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the best performer, answering 181 of 210 questions correctly. It states that the full report breaks down correct answers by subject matter and provides cost, duration, and human-performance comparisons, but the supplied text does not provide those comparative figures or identify the winning model's dated version.
qs: The best performer was Antropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet which answered 181 questions correctly out of 210 possible questions.
The full report also contains a breakdown of the number of correct answers by subject matter, cost, duration, and compared to human performance.

kp.k: Repository expands beyond the original study
kp.d: The authors distinguish the original paper's code, associated with the October 24th, 2024 initial commit, from an evolving repository that adds models. The displayed model list extends beyond the methodology's stated 16 models and includes Grok. New results are added separately, while the original paper's data file is explicitly identified.
qs: To view the code the original paper [url TBD] was run on please look at the initial commit from October 24th, 2024.
This repository is updated with new models as they come out.
As I continue to run more models I will put the results in the "Results" folder.
"NCBE MBE Questions_Answer_HumanChecked.csv" is the original file that the paper was based on.

kp.k: Single prompt and single run limit performance conclusions
kp.d: The authors identify reliance on one prompt template and one execution of the analysis as areas for follow-up. They suggest that different prompting might improve performance and that repeated runs with averaged results could mitigate output variation; these are proposed possibilities, not tested findings.
qs: Only one prompt template was used for the analysis. Different prompt engineering might yield better performance.
The analysis was conducted only once. Generative AI can produce varying results for the same prompt.
Running the analysis multiple times and averaging the results could mitigate this variation.

kp.k: Sampling settings remain an untested source of variation
kp.d: The analysis used temperature zero and top-p 0.2. The authors hypothesize that different models might respond differently to adjusted settings and propose testing alternative values in future studies.
qs: The analysis used a temperature of zero and a top-p of 0.2.
Different models might perform differently with adjusted settings.
Future studies could explore various temperature and top-p values to test this hypothesis.

kp.k: Some Llama answers required interpretation and human checking
kp.d: The author reports difficulty obtaining single-character answers from lower-level Llama models and describes using ChatGPT to determine the answer letter when handling problematic output. The author states that all these interpretations were manually checked for accuracy, documenting human verification within the benchmarking workflow.
qs: I had a lot of trouble with getting the lower level llama models to return a single character.
I eventually had to check to see if the answer was more than a character and if not then use ChatGPT to determine what the correct letter was.
All of these were manually checked for accuracy though.

kp.k: Safety configuration and hosting shaped the testing setup
kp.d: The author disabled Gemini's dangerous-content block because it flagged material as potentially offensive. Llama models were accessed through DeepInfra rather than run locally; the author suggests a different setup could reduce cost and time. Gemini models initially accessed through '-latest' aliases were subsequently relabeled with the stable models those aliases pointed to.
qs: I had to turn off Gemini's dangerous content block as it would flag it as potentially offensive.
Llama is more traditionally known as an LLM that you can launch on a local machine but we are using a service that hosts several llama models call DeepInfra.
A different set up could lower costs and time.
For Gemini models I used the "-latest" models which I later went back and changed to the stable model they were pointing towards.

kp.k: Question ownership restricts public release of benchmark inputs
kp.d: The authors state that the MBE questions cannot be publicly included because they belong to the NCBE, although they can be purchased. Study results and graph-generation code are provided in repository folders, separating available outputs and analysis code from the restricted question inputs.
qs: The MBE questions from this study cannot be included publically because they belong to the National Conference of Bar Examiners.
The results of the study are located in the folder results.
The graphs and code to generate the graphs are located in the folder Create Graphs.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The study authors report that Claude 3.5 Sonnet was the strongest performer in their multiple-choice MBE benchmark, answering 181 of 210 questions correctly.
pts.d: The William S. Richardson School of Law study, attributed to Matthew Stubenberg, Chloe Berridge, Thomas Fuerst Smith and Joshua Casey, makes a narrow claim about comparative AI performance on bar-exam questions. It does not claim that this performance establishes competence to practise law, replaces lawyers, or changes legal-service costs or employment. The authors also suggest that different prompts and generation settings might improve or change benchmark performance, and that repeated runs could mitigate variation. These are proposed avenues for research, not reported findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a single-run benchmark using 210 NCBE sample MBE questions, with results and code referenced in the repository.
pts.d: The methodology describes an initial study of 16 models from OpenAI, Google, Meta and Anthropic, while the evolving repository lists additional models and Grok. The supplied text reports the winning score but not the full comparative results. It refers readers to a full report for subject-level accuracy, cost, duration and human comparisons; those findings are not supplied here. Copyrighted questions are not publicly included. The first-person notes describe using ChatGPT to extract answer letters from problematic lower-level Llama responses and manually checking those extractions; this is answer-processing verification, not evidence of reliable legal advice.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported ranking is tied to the study's tested models and experimental setup, not a forecast of enduring model superiority.
pts.d: The repository identifies its October 24, 2024 initial commit as the code used for the original paper and states that new models are continually added. The results paragraph does not specify which dated Claude 3.5 Sonnet version achieved the reported score. Qualifications include one prompt template, one run, temperature zero and top-p 0.2. Operational conditions include disabling Gemini's dangerous-content block and hosting Llama through DeepInfra. The author suggests that another Llama setup could reduce costs and time, but supplies no quantified estimate or future deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct relevance is to researchers and users comparing AI models for multiple-choice legal-exam tasks; wider effects on legal-service participants are not stated.
pts.d: The project offers a comparative benchmark and an updated dashboard for those assessing model performance on MBE questions. Its findings concern tested systems and benchmark administration, including potential changes in accuracy, cost and runtime under different configurations. The source does not identify effects on law-firm staffing, legal-service buyers, clients, access to justice or the public. Although human performance comparisons are said to appear in the full report, the supplied text gives no results from which to extract a claim about lawyers or bar candidates.
